sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`docker run` creates and starts a container from an image. The image supplies the filesystem and default command, while flags select runtime settings such as published ports, environment values, mounted data, resource limits, and the container name.

The Go process runs inside the container's namespaces and uses the host kernel. An exposed image port is documentation; `-p 8080:8080` publishes a host port to the container port so traffic can reach the server.

For example, `docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env api:1.4` starts the image, maps host port 8080, and removes the stopped container. The service must listen on port 8080 inside the container.

Published ports may be reachable beyond localhost depending on the bind address and firewall. Containers are not a secret store, durable disk by default, or a replacement for graceful application shutdown.

Run a Go image when testing the exact packaged artifact or deploying it on a container host. Bind the server to a container-reachable address such as `:8080`, provide configuration at runtime, and set a restart or orchestration policy outside the binary.

sections.title: The core model: running a Go binary in Docker
sections.content:
running a Go binary in Docker is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Running the image turns static build content into a process with a network and storage boundary. Docker chooses a writable container layer, applies mounts and environment values, creates network interfaces, and starts the configured entrypoint. Port publishing has two numbers: the host-side port clients use and the container-side port where the server listens. Binding the host side to `127.0.0.1` can limit local exposure, while an unspecified host address may publish more broadly. Container names and restart settings belong to operations, not application identity. Logs should normally go to standard output and error so the runtime can collect them. State that must survive a container replacement belongs in a named volume or external service. Shutdown in Go follows the same process lifecycle: receive `SIGTERM`, stop accepting new requests, let in-flight work finish within a deadline, and then exit.

sections.title: running a Go binary in Docker example
sections.content:
~~~sh
docker run --rm \
  --name catalog-api \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  --env-file .env \
  catalog-api:1.4.0
~~~

sections.title: running a Go binary in Docker at a glance
sections.content:
| Setting | Meaning | Common confusion |
|---|---|---|
| Image name/tag | Artifact to instantiate | A tag is mutable unless a digest is used |
| `-p host:container` | Network publication | `EXPOSE` alone does not publish |
| `--env-file` | Runtime configuration | It is not encryption |
| Volume or bind mount | External persistent/shared path | Container writable layer is disposable |
